prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, bringing many-atom interrogation to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B029 (IceCube) to B012 (optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye). As Secretary I ask first whether the discovery is shown to be groundbreaking and only then who deserves credit. On the science, B012 now passes my test. The magic-wavelength lattice is a single clear idea, quantitatively understood, and what has been measured is a result about nature as well as an instrument: the gravitational redshift resolved across a millimetre-scale sample and agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level, reproduced in several laboratories. That is a clue from nature, not a theory. I came into this round saying that I regard the promised payoffs (varying constants, dark-matter searches, the redefinition of the second) as still ahead, and I still do, but the redshift and cross-laboratory agreement are already delivered and are enough for me. On credit, all seven members who proposed names for B012 chose the same two, and the chair's summary shows no one arguing for a third. The citation should be narrow: the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation, which the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize did not cover. It should say that the lattice-clock concept and early strontium demonstrations are Katori's and that the accuracy, systematics and many-body results are Ye's, without claiming general metrology.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against B012 is still the one I raised in round 1: it rewards a measurement technology, with its fundamental-physics payoffs prospective, and it follows the 2005 and 2012 prizes in neighbouring territory. I also cannot rule out that the 2001 to 2005 priority record (Lemonde and SYRTE, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Boyd) would support a different set of names than the one the committee holds; I am working from the round-1 statements and not from a checked record. The case against my former choice, B029, is in effect conceded: the chair's question asked for a diffuse-flux citation and a defensible trio from a collaboration of hundreds with AMANDA and Baikal predecessors, and I cannot supply evidence on who made the decisive contributions that would answer Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson. Pearce, who ranked IceCube first at the opening, now treats it as a candidate for a later year. A prize I cannot name with confidence should not be my lead this year, however much I like the discovery.

responses.point: Pearce moved from IceCube to B012 on the record and the attribution, and now describes B029 as a candidate for a later year because sources beyond TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane remain few and credit is spread over Baikal, AMANDA and a very large collaboration.
responses.response: You answered my own chair-question before the chair asked it. I argued that the diffuse flux alone supports a citation, and I still think that is true of the science, but you are right that the credit does not close, and your point about Baikal and AMANDA is one I cannot answer from the documents. I follow you to B012 for the same reason you give: the choice rests on the attribution and the record and not on the count of supporters. I would keep B029 as a first alternative, with the explicit understanding that it needs a credit analysis, for a later year, and not a rescue at this stage.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 as a clean invention with experimentally decisive demonstrations, disclosed his lineage through John Hall's laboratory, and also flags that the ion-clock lineage and ultrastable-laser work behind clock stability are left out of the credited names.
responses.response: In round 1 I said much the same as you about tool versus discovery, and I have not abandoned the distinction, but I now think the millimetre redshift and the 1e-18 cross-laboratory agreement answer it: those are measurements of nature that no earlier method could make. On your ion-clock and stabilized-laser point, I would not widen the names, since the three-person limit and the clean pair both argue against it, but the citation text can acknowledge the neutral-atom lattice specifically so that it does not read as a verdict on Al+ or Yb+ clocks. On your lineage through Hall, a disclosure in the record seems proportionate to me, because you report no joint work or financial interest with Katori or Ye, and I do not think it requires recusal. That is my view as a colleague, not a ruling on procedure.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B012 because the criteria are met on the record, asks that the citation be written narrowly around the lattice-clock concept and its realization, and notes that the 1e-18 and redshift results belong to Ye's group.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow wording, and I think the citation above follows it. On the attribution of the results, I would not go as far as dividing the text so sharply that Katori's half reads as a mere proposal, because the first strontium lattice demonstrations are part of his record and that is what makes the pair an invention-plus-realization prize. Your own caution that you cannot settle exact priority dates from memory is mine too; I would not want the committee to treat the priority record as closed until it has been checked against the 2001 to 2005 papers. On your University of Tokyo fellowship, you report no collaboration with Katori, and I read it as a disclosure to record and not a bar.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B036 as a prediction-then-confirmation story, but names B012 as the first alternative, calls it the safer choice if the committee wants settled understanding, and acknowledges the unresolved pairing mechanism and credit questions around Cao, Fatemi, Dean and Young.
responses.response: Your story is the one closest to my own taste, since a quantitative prediction was followed by a surprise from nature, and I told you in round 1 that I would not oppose B036 in a later year. I have not changed that. Your own file puts the weight on the question you ask yourself: how settled the understanding needs to be. By your standard, and by mine, B012 is the case where both the physics and the credit are settled today. If the committee decides this year, I would ask you whether you can accept B012 as a prize you do not need to block, and I would be glad to see B036 return with the credit among MacDonald, Bistritzer and the experimental first authors worked out.

responses.point: Mehlig moved B012 above his own first choice, B057, on the grounds that B057 has a real attribution gap and B012 does not, while still listing the pre-2005 priority record and the 2005 and 2012 lineage as uncertainties.
responses.response: I agree with your logic of putting a prize with a clean credit above one with a gap. In round 1 I asked you whether the Z2 classification alone could carry B057 and you moved on, so I take it that you have answered that for yourself. On your concern that a prize might be better timed after the redefinition of the second, I side with you, Olsson and Pearce that the demonstrated science alone is the criterion; waiting for a standards-body decision would make us dependent on a process that is not ours. I take your point on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and the narrow citation is the answer I can offer.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record from 2001 to 2005 (Katori, Lemonde and SYRTE, Takamoto, Ye, Ludlow, Hinkley) supports exactly Katori and Ye; I am relying on the round-1 statements and not on a checked record.
Whether the committee will accept the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice as distinct enough from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the narrow wording is sufficient.

Whether B012, a measurement technology, is a discovery of nature in the sense I normally ask for; I rest it on the delivered redshift and the 1e-18 cross-laboratory agreement, not on the prospective payoffs.

Whether B029 can be made nameable in a later year, since I have no evidence on the decisive contributions among IceCube, AMANDA and Baikal that would answer the concerns of Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile, and none of Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Halzen, Karle or Spiering is a supervisor, mentor or frequent co-author of mine. My connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet) are in string theory and tie to no shortlisted ballot. My change of lead from B029 to B012 is not driven by any new connection; I note that, as a co-opted Secretary, my voting status is not documented in my own profile.
